label: Chapter 2: Dukes, Guilds and the Grand Place, 1100 to 1430

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, I want to start with a bet.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Grand Place. I bet it began as a field of mud.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You're learning.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ha! Finally.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But we'll get to it. First, the family that rules the place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the twelfth century, Brussels falls into the hands of the counts of Leuven, and they just keep climbing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They become dukes of Lower Lotharingia, and then, as that old title stops meaning anything, dukes of Brabant.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brabant is a big deal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the richest territories in northwest Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It stretched across the heart of what's now Belgium and part of the southern Netherlands, with great towns like Leuven, Antwerp, and Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For a long time, Leuven is the leading city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But gradually the dukes start spending more time in Brussels, in a castle on a hill called the Coudenberg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which means?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Cold hill.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Cold hill. I love how nobody in this region tried to oversell anything.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Swamp, cold hill. They called it as they saw it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the dukes move in. And?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And by the late Middle Ages, Brussels is the main seat of the dukes, and with the dukes come money, officials, and prestige.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the dukes can't be the only reason it grows.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No. Brussels owes just as much to its own people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The town makes cloth. Wool comes in from England, weavers and dyers turn it into fabric, merchants sell it across Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And around that grows everything else.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brewing, baking, butchery, metalwork, carpentry, and eventually luxury goods like tapestries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the people doing those jobs organized themselves.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Into guilds. Part trade union, part business association, part social club, part political party.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So, basically, a LinkedIn group, but with swords.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not quite. But I'm going to think about that.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So where does the Grand Place come in?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the center of it all is the market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Down in the valley, on low ground by the river, there's an open space called the Lower Market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Traders set up stalls, townspeople do business.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the centuries, wooden stalls turn into stone halls, and the guilds build meeting houses around the edges.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it did begin as a muddy field.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It did. By the end of the thirteenth century, the drapers' guild has its own hall there, and the foundation of the square's future is laid.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Who actually runs the town?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A narrow elite. A handful of wealthy families, known as the Seven Lineages of Brussels, who hold the city council and the best offices.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Below them are the guilds, which have economic muscle but very little say in government.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, that's going to end well.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It does not end well. But first we meet one of the great documents of Brussels history.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1355, the Duke of Brabant, John the Third, dies without a male heir.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His eldest daughter, Joanna, becomes duchess.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And her husband is a man listeners of our Luxembourg episode will remember.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Wenceslas of Luxembourg, half brother of the Emperor Charles the Fourth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh! Small world.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a very small world. Everyone is somebody's half brother.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So what happens?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In January of 1356, before they can take up their rule, Joanna and Wenceslas have to sign a charter promising to respect the rights of the towns and nobles of Brabant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's called the Joyous Entry, named for the ceremonial entry a new ruler made into the cities of the duchy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Joyous Entry. It sounds like a party.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a contract. A very polite contract.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It limits the power of the duke.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He can't declare war, sign treaties, or raise taxes without the consent of the estates.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it even includes a remarkable clause allowing the people of Brabant to withdraw their obedience if the duke breaks the rules.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That sounds like the Magna Carta.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: People often compare them. Historians do caution that its later reputation was somewhat inflated by romantic writers in the nineteenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it remained an important symbol for centuries, and Brabantine rulers swore to uphold it for generations.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I'm guessing someone tested it right away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Immediately. Louis of Male, the Count of Flanders, a powerful neighbor with his own claim to Brabant, invades and seizes Brussels in 1356.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That was fast.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But he doesn't hold it long. A citizen named Everard t'Serclaes, from one of the great families, leads a night raid with a small band of men, slips into the city, and drives out the Flemish garrison.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that's a folk hero.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Absolutely. He's killed by a rival lord a few decades later, and today there's a bronze monument to him lying against a wall just off the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: According to local custom, rubbing the bronze arm of the statue brings good luck.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I'll bet it's polished bright.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's shining. Generations of hands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Anna, stubbornness tally?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, a night raid against an occupying army?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Two. Easily two.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now, the liberation helps fuel another great project.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city is growing quickly, and the old walls are too small.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between 1356 and 1383, the people of Brussels build a second, much larger ring of walls, with seven main gates and dozens of towers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a huge undertaking for a town that size.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It encloses about eight kilometers of ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Most of it is torn down in the nineteenth century, and its path is now traced by a ring of boulevards around the old center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Petite Ceinture. The small ring.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So if I look at a map of central Brussels, that five-sided shape of boulevards is the medieval city?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly. And one gate survives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The heavy, castle-like Porte de Hal, on the southern side of the ring.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. And the Town Hall. That's from this period too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The early fifteenth century is the great age of civic building.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1402, work begins on the Brussels Town Hall, on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The left wing goes up first, and the right wing follows in the fourteen-forties.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1449, the architects begin the soaring tower, a lace of stone rising about ninety-six meters, topped by a gilded statue of Saint Michael slaying the dragon.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's a famous quirk.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There is. The tower isn't centered over the main doorway, and the two wings are slightly different lengths.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: According to an old story, the architect was so horrified by the asymmetry that he threw himself from the tower.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh no.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians think that's just a legend.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Thank goodness. Although, it's a very dramatic way to say "I should have measured twice."

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is a good legend.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then there's the smallest landmark in the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Manneken Pis. A fountain figure of a little boy relieving himself into a basin, first mentioned in a document from 1388.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bronze you can visit today is a copy of a version made in 1619 by the sculptor Jérôme Duquesnoy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It stands on a street corner a few minutes from the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And he has a wardrobe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Well over a thousand costumes, changed on special occasions.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A thousand outfits! He's a small bronze boy with a better closet than me.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And lots of legends try to explain him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In one, a small duke of Leuven, hung in a basket from a tree during a battle, relieves himself on the enemy and inspires his soldiers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In another, a boy puts out a burning fuse and saves the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So which is true?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nobody knows. And Brussels doesn't seem to mind.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which is the right attitude, honestly.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, but now the tension between the lineages and the guilds.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Boils over. In 1421, a group of guildsmen, angry about the patricians' control of the government and rising taxes, storm the town hall, and several city magistrates are killed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The duke, John the Fourth, steps in to restore order.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the result is a victory for the craftsmen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So what changes?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From then on, the guilds, organized into nine groups called the Nations of Brussels, have a formal share of power on the city council.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the first time, Brussels has a government in which ordinary working people have a say.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a big deal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a very big deal. Out of a muddy marsh town, a real city is growing, with a strong sense of its own rights.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And money. Don't forget the money.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Never. And money is exactly what the next chapter is about.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Because in 1430, someone very rich and very ambitious walks in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Brussels becomes a capital.
